Counter metrics track database-specific performance indicators. CloudWatch integration enables alerting. Option B provides instance-level metrics only. Option C provides OS metrics, not database query performance. Option D requires database access and custom tooling.

stem: A DevOps team needs to implement automated capacity management that detects when EC2 instances are running out of disk space and automatically increases EBS volume sizes before applications are affected. What is the BEST approach?

options.text: Use CloudWatch agent on EC2 instances to publish disk usage metrics. Create CloudWatch alarms when disk usage exceeds 80%. The alarm triggers an SSM Automation document that: modifies the EBS volume size using the ModifyVolume API, waits for the modification to complete, then runs a command on the instance to extend the filesystem.
Use large EBS volumes from the start to avoid running out of space.
Monitor disk space manually via SSH.
Set up a cron job on each instance to check disk space.

explanation: CloudWatch agent provides custom disk metrics. Alarms trigger at threshold. SSM Automation handles the multi-step EBS resize process: API call to modify volume, wait for completion, filesystem extension command. This is fully automated and proactive. Option B wastes money. Option C is manual. Option D runs locally without centralized management.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to implement AWS WAF rules to protect an application from common web attacks. The rules must cover SQL injection, XSS, and known bad IP addresses, while minimizing false positives. What is the recommended approach?

options.text: Create an AWS WAF web ACL with AWS Managed Rules groups: AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet for general protection, AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet for SQL injection, AWSManagedRulesKnownBadInputsRuleSet for known exploit patterns, and AWSManagedRulesAmazonIpReputationList for bad IP blocking. Deploy initially in count mode to assess impact, then switch to block mode after tuning.
Write custom WAF rules for each attack type from scratch.
Use only rate-based rules to limit request volume.
Block all traffic from non-US IP addresses.

explanation: AWS Managed Rules provide pre-built, regularly updated protection rules maintained by AWS. Starting in count mode allows assessment and tuning before blocking traffic, minimizing false positives. Multiple managed rule groups provide layered protection. Option B requires security expertise and ongoing maintenance. Option C only addresses volumetric attacks. Option D blocks legitimate international traffic.

stem: A DevOps team needs to implement a release management process where multiple microservice teams can independently deploy their services, but production deployments require approval from a release manager. How should this be orchestrated?

options.text: Create separate CodePipelines for each microservice. Add a manual approval action before the production deployment stage in each pipeline. Configure the approval action to send notifications via SNS to the release manager with details about the changes. The release manager approves or rejects through the CodePipeline console or API.
Use a single monolithic pipeline for all microservices.
Allow all teams to deploy to production without approval.
Have a weekly release window where all services deploy together.

explanation: Separate pipelines allow independent team deployments. Manual approval actions gate production deployments while allowing autonomous pre-production deployments. SNS notifications keep the release manager informed. The approval can be automated via Lambda for certain criteria. Option B creates coupling between teams. Option C lacks governance. Option D reduces deployment frequency.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to implement a configuration management solution that allows changing application configuration without deploying new code or restarting services. Changes must be deployed gradually with automatic rollback if issues arise. Which AWS service BEST provides this?

options.text: Use AWS AppConfig to manage application configuration. Create a hosted configuration profile with the configuration data. Define a deployment strategy (linear or exponential) that gradually rolls out changes. Configure CloudWatch alarm-based automatic rollback. Use the AppConfig Agent in the application to poll for configuration updates.
Store configuration in SSM Parameter Store and restart services after changes.
Embed configuration in environment variables and redeploy.
Use a configuration file in S3 that services read at startup.

explanation: AppConfig provides managed configuration deployment with gradual rollout strategies and automatic rollback. The AppConfig Agent polls for updates without requiring restarts. Deployment strategies control the pace of rollout. CloudWatch alarms trigger rollback if issues arise. Option B requires restarts. Option C requires redeployment. Option D only reads at startup.

stem: A company runs an application that uses Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. They need to implement a read scaling strategy that handles variable read traffic while maintaining consistent read performance. The current read traffic varies from 1,000 to 50,000 queries per second throughout the day. What is the BEST approach?

options.text: Configure Aurora Auto Scaling to automatically add or remove Aurora read replicas based on the CPUUtilization metric or average connections. Set minimum and maximum replica counts. Use the Aurora reader endpoint to distribute read traffic across all available replicas automatically.
Provision the maximum number of read replicas permanently.
Use a single Aurora instance with a larger instance class.
Implement read-through caching in the application only.

explanation: Aurora Auto Scaling dynamically adjusts the number of read replicas based on demand metrics. The reader endpoint automatically distributes connections across replicas. Minimum/maximum counts ensure availability and cost control. Option B wastes resources during low traffic. Option C cannot scale reads independently. Option D does not address database-level scaling.

stem: A DevOps team needs to implement health checks for their microservices that go beyond simple TCP or HTTP checks. They need deep health checks that verify downstream dependencies (database, cache, external APIs) are functioning. How should this be implemented with ECS and ALB?

options.text: Implement a /health endpoint in each microservice that checks all downstream dependencies and returns a composite health status. Configure the ALB target group health check to use this endpoint. Set appropriate health check intervals, thresholds, and timeouts. Use CloudWatch alarms on UnHealthyHostCount for alerting.
Use TCP health checks on the application port.
Check only the HTTP status code of the main page.
Rely on ECS task health checks only.

explanation: A /health endpoint that checks downstream dependencies provides a comprehensive health view. If a database connection fails, the health check fails, and the ALB removes the instance from rotation. CloudWatch alarms on UnHealthyHostCount provide alerting. Option B only verifies the port is open. Option C does not check dependencies. Option D only checks container status.

stem: A DevOps engineer receives alerts about high Lambda function throttling. The function is triggered by an SQS queue and processes financial transactions. They need to resolve the throttling without losing any messages. What is the CORRECT approach?

options.text: Request a Lambda concurrent execution limit increase via AWS Support. Configure the SQS trigger with a reduced batch size and maximum concurrency setting to control the Lambda invocation rate. Set up a dead-letter queue on the SQS source queue to capture messages that fail after maximum retries. Review and optimize the Lambda function code to reduce execution duration.
Delete the throttled messages and reprocess later.
Switch from SQS to SNS for triggering the Lambda function.
Increase the Lambda function timeout to reduce throttling.

explanation: Increasing the concurrency limit addresses the throttling directly. Reduced batch size and maximum concurrency settings on the SQS trigger control the invocation rate. SQS automatically retries throttled messages. A DLQ captures permanently failed messages. Code optimization reduces execution time and concurrency needs. Option B loses messages. Option C does not solve throttling. Option D does not affect concurrency.

stem: A company needs to implement data loss prevention (DLP) for their S3 buckets containing sensitive data. They need to automatically discover and classify sensitive data, and prevent it from being made publicly accessible. Which combination of AWS services provides this?

options.text: Use Amazon Macie to automatically discover and classify sensitive data (PII, financial data, credentials) in S3 buckets. Configure Macie to publish findings to EventBridge. Create EventBridge rules that trigger Lambda functions to apply remediation (adding bucket policies to block public access, adding encryption). Use S3 Block Public Access at the account level as a preventive control.
Manually review S3 bucket contents for sensitive data.
Use AWS Config rules for S3 public access only.
Encrypt all S3 data without classification.

explanation: Macie uses ML to discover and classify sensitive data automatically. EventBridge with Lambda automates remediation based on findings. S3 Block Public Access provides an account-level preventive control. Together they provide discovery, classification, detection, and prevention. Option B is manual and unscalable. Option C checks access but not data classification. Option D encrypts without understanding what data exists.

stem: A DevOps engineer is implementing a deployment strategy for an application that requires zero-downtime deployments with the ability to instantly roll back. The application runs on EC2 instances behind an ALB and uses an RDS database. Which deployment strategy provides the FASTEST rollback?

options.text: Implement Blue/Green deployments using CodeDeploy. The green environment runs the new version alongside the blue environment. CodeDeploy reroutes ALB traffic from blue to green. If issues arise, CodeDeploy instantly reroutes traffic back to blue. Ensure database changes are backward-compatible.
Use rolling deployments with CodeDeploy.
Use in-place deployments with a single target group.
Deploy to a new Auto Scaling group and swap DNS records.

explanation: Blue/Green deployment provides the fastest rollback because both versions are running simultaneously. Traffic rerouting via ALB is instant (no need to redeploy code). Backward-compatible database changes ensure both versions can work with the same schema. Option B requires redeploying the previous version. Option C requires full redeployment for rollback. Option D requires DNS propagation time.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to manage Kubernetes resources on Amazon EKS using infrastructure as code. They want to manage both AWS resources (VPC, EKS cluster) and Kubernetes resources (deployments, services, config maps) in a single IaC framework. Which approach is MOST unified?

options.text: Use AWS CDK with the aws-eks module to provision the EKS cluster and its underlying AWS infrastructure. Use CDK8s (CDK for Kubernetes) to define Kubernetes manifests as code. Integrate the CDK8s output into the CDK EKS cluster construct using cluster.addCdk8sChart() to deploy both AWS and K8s resources together.
Use Terraform for AWS resources and kubectl for Kubernetes resources.
Use CloudFormation for AWS resources and Helm for Kubernetes resources.
Use eksctl for cluster management and separate YAML manifests.

explanation: CDK with CDK8s provides a unified TypeScript/Python framework for both AWS and Kubernetes resources. CDK manages the cluster and AWS infrastructure, CDK8s generates Kubernetes manifests, and addCdk8sChart() integrates them. This provides a single deployment pipeline and language. Option B requires two tools. Option C requires two tools. Option D lacks IaC integration.

stem: A company runs a video processing application that uses Amazon S3 for input/output and AWS Lambda for processing. Large video files (up to 10 GB) need to be processed reliably. Lambda's 15-minute timeout and ephemeral storage limits are concerns. How should this be architected for resilience?

options.text: Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the processing workflow. Split the processing into multiple Lambda functions that each handle a portion of the work (download segment, transcode, upload segment). Use S3 for intermediate storage between steps. Configure Step Functions error handling with retry policies and catch blocks for each step. Use Lambda with 10 GB ephemeral storage for large file segments.
Use a single Lambda function with maximum timeout and memory.
Process videos directly on EC2 instances without orchestration.
Use Amazon Elastic Transcoder for all processing.

explanation: Step Functions orchestrates the workflow with built-in error handling and retries. Breaking processing into segments with S3 intermediate storage handles the timeout limitation. Lambda's 10 GB ephemeral storage handles large segments. Step Functions retry policies handle transient failures. Option B may timeout for large files. Option C lacks orchestration and error handling. Option D is limited in capabilities.

stem: A company runs a multi-tenant SaaS application and needs to implement per-tenant monitoring. They need to track each tenant's resource usage, performance, and costs separately. How should the monitoring be structured?

options.text: Use CloudWatch custom metrics with a TenantId dimension on all application metrics. Create per-tenant CloudWatch dashboards using metric filtering on the TenantId dimension. Use CloudWatch Embedded Metric Format (EMF) in the application to efficiently publish high-cardinality tenant metrics. Set up CloudWatch Contributor Insights to identify top tenants by resource usage.
Create separate AWS accounts for each tenant.
Use a single aggregate dashboard for all tenants.
Store per-tenant metrics in a DynamoDB table.

explanation: Custom metrics with TenantId dimension enable per-tenant filtering and dashboards. EMF provides efficient high-cardinality metric publication without individual PutMetricData API calls. Contributor Insights identifies the highest-consuming tenants automatically. Option B is expensive and complex. Option C lacks tenant-level visibility. Option D does not integrate with CloudWatch alerting.

stem: A company detects that an IAM access key has been exposed in a public GitHub repository. The key belongs to a service account used by production applications. What is the correct incident response sequence?

options.text: Immediately create a new access key for the IAM user and update all applications to use the new key. Then deactivate (do not delete) the exposed access key to preserve it for forensic analysis. Review CloudTrail logs for any unauthorized API calls made with the exposed key. Rotate all other credentials that may have been accessible by the compromised key. Finally, implement preventive measures like GitHub secret scanning and pre-commit hooks.
Delete the IAM user account immediately.
Delete the exposed key and wait to see if anything breaks.
Report the incident but take no immediate action.

explanation: The correct sequence creates new credentials first to maintain application availability, then deactivates (not deletes) the exposed key for forensic analysis. CloudTrail review identifies unauthorized access. Credential rotation addresses potential lateral movement. Preventive measures prevent recurrence. Option B causes application outage. Option C may break applications and deletes evidence. Option D allows continued unauthorized access.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to implement a secure architecture for Lambda functions that access resources in a VPC (RDS database, ElastiCache). The Lambda functions must also be able to access AWS services (S3, DynamoDB) and the internet for third-party API calls. What is the correct network configuration?

options.text: Configure Lambda functions to run in private subnets with VPC access. Create VPC endpoints for AWS services (S3 gateway endpoint, DynamoDB gateway endpoint, other interface endpoints as needed). Deploy a NAT gateway in a public subnet for internet access to third-party APIs. Configure security groups on the Lambda ENIs to allow only necessary outbound traffic.
Run Lambda functions without VPC configuration and use VPC peering.
Deploy Lambda functions in public subnets with internet gateway access.
Use Lambda@Edge for all functions to avoid VPC restrictions.

explanation: Lambda in private subnets accesses VPC resources directly. VPC endpoints provide private connectivity to AWS services without internet routing. NAT gateway enables internet access for third-party APIs. Security groups control outbound traffic. Option B cannot access VPC resources. Option C is not supported (Lambda in public subnets still requires NAT for internet). Option D has different limitations and use cases.

stem: A DevOps engineer is implementing a deployment notification system. They need to send deployment status updates (started, succeeded, failed) to a Slack channel with details about the deployment including the commit message, deployer, and environment. Which approach is MOST integrated with AWS?

options.text: Use AWS Chatbot integrated with Slack. Configure CodePipeline to send notifications to an SNS topic. Connect the SNS topic to AWS Chatbot, which formats and delivers messages to the designated Slack channel with interactive pipeline controls.
Write a custom Lambda function to send Slack webhooks on pipeline events.
Send email notifications and forward them to Slack manually.
Check the CodePipeline console for deployment status.

explanation: AWS Chatbot provides native Slack integration with rich message formatting for AWS service notifications. CodePipeline notifications via SNS deliver deployment events automatically. Chatbot provides interactive controls to approve/reject actions directly from Slack. Option B requires custom code maintenance. Option C is manual. Option D requires console access.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to ensure that all CloudFormation stacks deployed in the organization comply with naming conventions, required tags, and resource configuration standards. The compliance checks must run before any stack is created or updated. Which approach provides preventive compliance?

options.text: Use AWS CloudFormation Hooks to register custom hook extensions that validate resource configurations before provisioning. Hooks intercept create and update operations and can block non-compliant resources. Configure the hooks to check naming conventions, required tags, and resource configurations.
Use AWS Config rules to detect non-compliant resources after creation.
Review all CloudFormation templates manually before deployment.
Use SCPs to restrict resource creation to specific configurations.

explanation: CloudFormation Hooks provide preventive controls that intercept resource operations before they execute. Hooks can validate naming conventions, tags, and configurations, and block non-compliant provisioning. This is a true pre-provisioning gate. Option B is detective, not preventive. Option C is manual. Option D has limited granularity for resource configuration checks.

stem: A company operates a SaaS platform that must meet 99.99% availability SLA. The application uses Aurora, ECS, and ElastiCache. Which architecture provides the highest availability?

options.text: Deploy across at least 3 Availability Zones. Use Aurora Multi-AZ with at least 2 read replicas across AZs. Deploy ECS tasks across all AZs with a minimum of 3 tasks. Use ElastiCache Redis with cluster mode enabled across AZs. Configure Route 53 health checks with failover to a static maintenance page. Implement circuit breakers and retry logic in the application.
Deploy across 2 Availability Zones with Multi-AZ for all services.
Use a single large EC2 instance with all services deployed on it.
Deploy only in us-east-1 with maximum instance sizes.

explanation: 99.99% availability requires 3+ AZs to survive AZ failures without capacity reduction. Multiple ECS tasks across AZs provide compute resilience. Aurora Multi-AZ with replicas provides database resilience. ElastiCache cluster mode distributes data across AZs. Circuit breakers prevent cascading failures. Route 53 health checks provide DNS-level failover. Option B with 2 AZs loses 50% capacity on AZ failure. Option C is a SPOF. Option D limits to one Region.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to implement compliance reporting that shows the security posture across all AWS accounts. The report should include compliance status of Config rules, Security Hub findings, and GuardDuty findings. Which approach provides the MOST automated reporting?

options.text: Enable AWS Security Hub with the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard across all accounts via AWS Organizations. Security Hub aggregates findings from Config, GuardDuty, Inspector, and other services. Use the Security Hub Insights feature for custom security posture reports. Export findings to S3 via EventBridge for long-term storage and use QuickSight for executive dashboards.
Create custom scripts to query Config, GuardDuty, and Security Hub separately.
Review each service's console individually for compliance status.
Use AWS Trusted Advisor for security reporting.

explanation: Security Hub provides centralized security posture management that aggregates findings from multiple AWS security services. Organization-wide deployment ensures coverage. Insights provide custom reporting. S3 export with QuickSight enables executive-level dashboards. Option B requires maintaining custom code. Option C is manual. Option D provides limited security checks.

stem: A company needs to implement automated remediation for common security findings from AWS Security Hub. Findings include unencrypted EBS volumes, public S3 buckets, and security groups with unrestricted SSH access. What is the MOST scalable remediation approach?

options.text: Use Security Hub's automated response and remediation feature with custom actions. Create EventBridge rules that match specific Security Hub finding types. Each rule triggers a specific SSM Automation document: one for encrypting EBS volumes (create encrypted copy, swap volumes), one for applying S3 bucket policies, and one for removing unrestricted SSH rules. Log all remediation actions to CloudWatch.
Remediate findings manually through the Security Hub console.
Write a single Lambda function that handles all finding types.
Disable the security standards to stop generating findings.

explanation: EventBridge rules matching Security Hub finding types provide event-driven remediation. Separate SSM Automation documents for each finding type ensure correct remediation logic. Logging provides audit trails. This scales across accounts and finding types. Option B is manual. Option C becomes a complex monolithic function. Option D removes security visibility.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to implement cross-account access to an Amazon ECR repository. A central shared services account hosts container images that must be pulled by ECS tasks in multiple application accounts. What is the correct configuration?

options.text: Configure an ECR repository policy in the shared services account that grants ecr:BatchGetImage, ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer, and ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability permissions to the IAM roles used by ECS tasks in the application accounts. In each application account, configure the ECS task execution role to have permissions to authenticate with ECR in the shared services account.
Replicate ECR images to each application account.
Make the ECR repository public.
Use Docker Hub instead of ECR for cross-account access.

explanation: ECR repository policies support cross-account access by granting specific permissions to IAM principals in other accounts. The ECS task execution role needs permissions to authenticate with the cross-account ECR. This provides secure, centralized image management. Option B creates multiple copies and management overhead. Option C exposes images publicly. Option D introduces an external dependency.

stem: A DevOps team wants to implement progressive delivery for their Kubernetes application on EKS. They need to support canary releases, A/B testing based on HTTP headers, and automated rollback based on metrics. Which tool integrates BEST with EKS for this?

options.text: Deploy Flagger (or Argo Rollouts) on the EKS cluster integrated with AWS App Mesh or an Ingress controller. Configure canary resources that define the traffic shifting strategy, analysis metrics (from CloudWatch or Prometheus), and rollback thresholds. Flagger automatically manages the progressive delivery lifecycle.
Use Kubernetes native rolling updates for all deployments.
Implement custom traffic splitting logic in the application code.
Use CodeDeploy for EKS deployments.

explanation: Flagger and Argo Rollouts are purpose-built for progressive delivery on Kubernetes. They integrate with service meshes (App Mesh) and ingress controllers for traffic management, support canary releases and A/B testing, and automate analysis and rollback based on metrics. Option B only supports rolling updates. Option C adds application complexity. Option D does not support header-based routing on EKS.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to implement a tagging strategy across all AWS resources. Tags must include mandatory fields (Environment, Team, CostCenter, Application) and follow specific naming conventions. How should this be enforced at scale?

options.text: Create an AWS Organizations tag policy that defines required tags and allowed values for each tag key. Enforce the tag policy across the organization. Complement with AWS Config rules (required-tags) that detect non-compliant resources and trigger SSM Automation remediation. Use SCPs to deny resource creation when required tags are missing using the aws:RequestTag condition.
Document the tagging policy in a wiki and trust teams to follow it.
Create IAM policies per user that require tags on resource creation.
Use a weekly script to scan and tag untagged resources.

explanation: Tag policies define the organization-wide standard. SCPs provide preventive enforcement by blocking untagged resource creation. Config rules provide detective controls with remediation for existing resources. This layered approach ensures comprehensive tag compliance. Option B relies on human compliance. Option C requires per-user management. Option D is reactive and periodic.

stem: A company needs to implement a global content delivery strategy for their application API. Users are distributed worldwide and experience high latency when accessing the API hosted in a single Region. Which approach provides the BEST balance of performance and simplicity?

options.text: Deploy the API behind Amazon CloudFront with API Gateway as the origin. Enable CloudFront caching for cacheable GET requests with appropriate TTLs. Use Lambda@Edge or CloudFront Functions for request/response manipulation. For non-cacheable requests, CloudFront still reduces latency through its global network and persistent connections to the origin.
Deploy the API in every AWS Region for lowest latency.
Use AWS Global Accelerator without caching.
Increase the API Gateway timeout to handle slow connections.

explanation: CloudFront reduces latency through its global edge network, caching cacheable responses close to users, and maintaining persistent connections to the origin for non-cacheable requests. Lambda@Edge handles dynamic request processing at the edge. This provides significant latency improvement with a single-Region backend. Option B requires managing multi-Region infrastructure. Option C improves routing but not caching. Option D does not reduce latency.

stem: A DevOps team needs to implement alerting that reduces false positives and alert fatigue. Their current monitoring generates too many individual alarms that overwhelm the on-call team. How should they restructure their alerting?

options.text: Implement CloudWatch Composite Alarms that combine multiple related metric alarms using AND/OR logic. Only trigger notifications when multiple conditions are met simultaneously (e.g., high CPU AND high error rate AND low request count). Configure different severity levels that route to different SNS topics for tiered escalation.
Reduce the number of alarms by removing most of them.
Increase alarm thresholds so fewer alarms trigger.
Send all alarms to a single email distribution list.

explanation: Composite alarms reduce false positives by requiring multiple conditions to be true before alerting. AND logic ensures alerts only fire when correlated signals confirm an actual issue. Tiered escalation routes alerts to appropriate teams based on severity. Option B may miss real issues. Option C delays detection. Option D does not reduce alert volume.

stem: A company's production database (Amazon RDS MySQL) is experiencing a sudden performance degradation. The DevOps team needs to quickly identify whether the issue is caused by increased query volume, slow queries, lock contention, or insufficient resources. What is the FASTEST diagnostic path?

options.text: Open RDS Performance Insights and analyze the database load by wait events to identify bottlenecks. Check the top SQL tab to find the queries consuming the most resources. Examine the database load by users/hosts to identify the source. Correlate with CloudWatch RDS metrics (CPU, connections, IOPS) to check resource utilization.
Connect to the database and run SHOW PROCESSLIST.
Check CloudWatch CPU and memory metrics only.
Restore from a backup and compare performance.

explanation: Performance Insights provides immediate visibility into database load by wait events (IO, locks, CPU), top SQL statements, and resource metrics. This quickly identifies whether the issue is query-based, lock-based, or resource-based. CloudWatch metrics complement with infrastructure-level data. Option B provides limited real-time view. Option C only shows infrastructure metrics. Option D is time-consuming and destructive.

stem: A company needs to implement a secure multi-account strategy using AWS Organizations. They need to prevent member accounts from leaving the organization, restrict which services can be used, and ensure security services are enabled in all accounts. Which TWO controls should be implemented?

options.text: Create SCPs that deny organizations:LeaveOrganization to prevent accounts from leaving. Create additional SCPs that deny actions for non-approved services using explicit deny statements.
Enable AWS Security Hub, GuardDuty, and CloudTrail as delegated administrator services from the management account, ensuring they are automatically enabled in all member accounts.
Use IAM policies in each account to restrict service usage.
Manually configure security services in each account.
Use VPC security groups to control service access.

explanation: SCPs provide organization-wide preventive controls that cannot be overridden by member account administrators. Denying LeaveOrganization prevents account escape. Service restrictions limit blast radius. Delegated administrator for security services ensures consistent security coverage with centralized management. Option C can be overridden by account admins. Option D is manual. Option E only controls network traffic.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to implement a deployment pipeline that supports both container-based (ECS) and serverless (Lambda) applications from a single monorepo. The pipeline should only build and deploy the application type that changed. What is the BEST architecture?

options.text: Create an EventBridge rule triggered by CodeCommit push events. Use a Lambda function to analyze the changed file paths using GetDifferences API. Based on the paths, the Lambda function triggers the appropriate CodePipeline: one for the ECS application (which includes CodeBuild for Docker image build and CodeDeploy for ECS deployment) and another for the Lambda application (which includes CodeBuild for SAM build and CloudFormation for SAM deployment).
Use a single pipeline that always builds and deploys both applications.
Split the monorepo into separate repositories.
Use CodeBuild with conditional logic to skip unchanged applications.

explanation: Lambda-based path analysis provides selective pipeline triggering. Separate pipelines for ECS and Lambda applications use appropriate deployment tools for each type. This avoids unnecessary builds and deployments while supporting both application types. Option B wastes resources. Option C requires repository restructuring. Option D puts pipeline logic in build scripts.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to implement a way to preview the impact of CloudFormation stack updates before executing them. They want to see which resources will be added, modified, or replaced. Which CloudFormation feature supports this?

options.text: Use CloudFormation Change Sets. Create a change set with the updated template, review the proposed changes including resource actions (Add, Modify, Replace, Remove), and decide whether to execute or delete the change set. Integrate change set creation and review into the CI/CD pipeline before execution.
Use CloudFormation drift detection to preview changes.
Deploy to a test stack first and compare resources.
Read the CloudFormation documentation to predict changes.

explanation: Change Sets show exactly what CloudFormation will do (Add, Modify, Replace, Remove) before executing. This allows review and approval of changes. Pipeline integration enables automated creation and manual review before execution. Option B detects existing drift, not proposed changes. Option C duplicates infrastructure. Option D is unreliable.

stem: A company runs a data lake on Amazon S3 with critical data that must be protected against accidental deletion. They also need to be able to recover objects to any point in time within the last 30 days. Which S3 features should be configured?

options.text: Enable S3 Versioning to maintain all object versions. Enable S3 Object Lock in Governance mode with a 30-day retention period to prevent accidental deletion. Configure lifecycle rules to expire non-current versions after 30 days for cost optimization. Enable MFA Delete for an additional layer of protection against deletion.
Use S3 Cross-Region Replication as the only backup.
Take daily snapshots of the S3 bucket.
Store data in S3 Glacier for protection.

explanation: Versioning maintains all object versions for point-in-time recovery. Object Lock in Governance mode prevents accidental deletion while allowing authorized overrides. Lifecycle rules manage non-current version costs. MFA Delete adds an extra deletion protection layer. Option B protects against Region failure but not accidental deletion. Option C is not an S3 feature. Option D is for archival, not protection.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to track and visualize the deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and mean time to recovery (MTTR) for their CI/CD pipeline. These are the DORA metrics. How should this be implemented using AWS services?

options.text: Publish custom CloudWatch metrics from CodePipeline execution events using EventBridge and Lambda. Track deployment frequency from pipeline execution counts, lead time from commit timestamp to deployment completion, change failure rate from deployment failures and rollbacks, and MTTR from failure detection to resolution. Create a CloudWatch dashboard to visualize all four DORA metrics.
Count deployments manually in a spreadsheet.
Use CodePipeline's built-in metrics only.
Deploy a third-party DevOps analytics platform.

explanation: Custom CloudWatch metrics from pipeline events capture all four DORA metrics. EventBridge captures CodePipeline state changes. Lambda calculates derived metrics (lead time, failure rate). CloudWatch dashboards provide visualization. This is fully integrated with AWS services. Option B is manual. Option C provides limited pipeline metrics, not DORA metrics. Option D adds external dependency.

stem: A company needs to implement automated response to AWS Health events that affect their resources. When AWS reports a scheduled maintenance event for an EC2 instance, the system should automatically migrate the instance before the maintenance window. What is the correct implementation?

options.text: Create an EventBridge rule that matches AWS Health events for EC2 scheduled maintenance. The rule triggers a Lambda function or SSM Automation document that: identifies affected instances, creates AMIs from the instances, launches replacement instances from the AMIs, updates target group registrations, and terminates the original instances before the maintenance window.
Wait for AWS to perform the maintenance automatically.
Check the AWS Health Dashboard manually each day.
Enable EC2 auto-recovery for all instances.

explanation: EventBridge captures AWS Health events proactively. Automated migration before the maintenance window ensures zero downtime from the user perspective. The automation handles the full lifecycle: backup, replace, register, cleanup. Option B may cause brief downtime during maintenance. Option C is manual and may miss events. Option D handles unexpected failures but not scheduled maintenance proactively.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to implement a secure method for EC2 instances and containers to access secrets and configuration without using long-lived credentials. The solution must work for both EC2 and ECS Fargate workloads. What is the BEST approach?

options.text: Use IAM roles for EC2 instances and ECS task roles to provide temporary credentials automatically. Access secrets from AWS Secrets Manager using the IAM role's permissions. For ECS, configure task role and task execution role separately: execution role for pulling images and secrets injection, task role for application-level AWS API access.
Store AWS access keys in environment variables on each instance.
Use a shared IAM user with access keys distributed to all services.
Store credentials in the application configuration files on EBS volumes.

explanation: IAM roles provide automatic temporary credential rotation. EC2 instance profiles and ECS task roles deliver credentials through the instance metadata service. Secrets Manager provides secret retrieval with IAM authentication. ECS separates execution role (infrastructure) from task role (application) for least privilege. Option B uses long-lived credentials. Option C shares credentials. Option D stores credentials on disk.

stem: A DevOps team uses AWS CodePipeline with multiple stages including source, build, test, staging deploy, integration test, and production deploy. They want to ensure that if any stage fails, the team is notified and the failure is tracked. Additionally, they want to prevent the same artifact from being re-tested if it has already passed all tests. How should this be implemented?

options.text: Configure CodePipeline notification rules that send events to SNS for stage failures and pipeline completions. Use pipeline execution IDs and artifact revisions to track which versions have been tested. Implement a CodeBuild cache or DynamoDB table that records tested artifact hashes to skip redundant test execution for previously tested artifacts.
Check the pipeline console for failures manually.
Re-run all tests for every pipeline execution regardless.
Use CodePipeline webhooks for all notifications.

explanation: CodePipeline notification rules provide automated event delivery for stage transitions. Artifact tracking with DynamoDB or S3 prevents redundant testing by checking if the current artifact revision has already been tested successfully. This optimizes pipeline execution time. Option B is manual. Option C wastes time and resources. Option D has been replaced by notification rules.

stem: A DevOps engineer is managing a complex CloudFormation template that has grown to over 500 resources. The template is becoming difficult to maintain and deploy. What is the BEST strategy to improve manageability?

options.text: Refactor the template into nested stacks, grouping related resources (networking, compute, database, monitoring) into separate child templates. Use the parent stack to orchestrate child stacks and pass outputs between them. Store child templates in S3 and reference them via TemplateURL. Use cross-stack references for shared resources.
Keep everything in a single template but add more comments.
Split into separate independent stacks with no references between them.
Migrate to a different IaC tool.

explanation: Nested stacks break down complexity while maintaining orchestration through the parent stack. Related resources are grouped logically. Cross-stack references enable communication between stacks. S3-hosted child templates allow independent versioning. Option B does not reduce complexity. Option C loses resource relationships. Option D is not necessary.

stem: A company needs to implement a queue-based load leveling pattern for their order processing system. During peak hours, the order volume can spike to 10x normal levels. The processing backend cannot scale instantly. How should this be architectured?

options.text: Place an SQS queue between the API Gateway frontend and the processing backend. API Gateway sends orders to SQS immediately (fast response to users). The backend ECS service processes messages from SQS at its own rate. Configure SQS visibility timeout and dead-letter queues. Use ECS auto-scaling based on the SQS ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible metric to scale the processing backend gradually.
Provision the backend to handle peak traffic permanently.
Return errors to users during peak traffic.
Use API Gateway throttling to limit incoming requests.

explanation: SQS decouples the frontend from the backend, absorbing traffic spikes without losing orders. The backend processes messages at its sustainable rate. SQS-based auto-scaling gradually increases backend capacity based on queue depth. DLQ handles failed messages. Option B wastes resources during normal hours. Option C loses orders. Option D rejects valid orders.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to implement log analysis for security auditing. They need to query CloudTrail logs across multiple accounts to find specific API actions, identify who made changes, and detect unusual activity patterns. What is the MOST cost-effective approach for ad-hoc querying?

options.text: Configure CloudTrail to deliver logs to a central S3 bucket from all accounts. Use Amazon Athena with a CloudTrail-specific table definition to query the logs using standard SQL. Create saved queries for common audit patterns (unauthorized API calls, resource deletions, IAM changes). Use Athena workgroups to control query costs.
Stream all CloudTrail logs to CloudWatch Logs and use Logs Insights.
Load all CloudTrail logs into Amazon OpenSearch for searching.
Download CloudTrail logs and search them locally.

explanation: Athena provides serverless, cost-effective SQL querying directly on S3 data. You only pay for data scanned. Partitioned CloudTrail data in S3 reduces scan costs. Saved queries enable reusable audit patterns. Workgroups control query costs. Option B is expensive for long-term log storage. Option C requires provisioned infrastructure. Option D is manual and unscalable.

stem: A DevOps team manages a production application that occasionally experiences sudden traffic drops that indicate a potential issue. They need to detect when traffic drops below a baseline and automatically investigate potential causes. What is the BEST monitoring approach?

options.text: Create a CloudWatch anomaly detection alarm on the RequestCount or InvocationCount metric. When traffic drops below the expected lower band, trigger a Step Functions workflow that: checks Route 53 health status, verifies ALB target health, tests API endpoints, checks upstream dependencies, and compiles a diagnostic report sent to the operations team via SNS.
Set a static alarm for low traffic values.
Check traffic dashboards periodically during business hours.
Use access logs to detect traffic drops after the fact.

explanation: Anomaly detection accounts for expected traffic patterns (time of day, weekday vs weekend) and detects unexpected drops. Step Functions automates the investigation workflow checking multiple potential causes. This provides fast detection and root cause identification. Option B may false-alarm during normal low-traffic periods. Option C misses off-hours issues. Option D is reactive.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to implement a centralized logging architecture that ensures log integrity and prevents tampering, even by administrators. The solution must meet SOC 2 and PCI DSS audit requirements. Which architecture provides the strongest integrity guarantees?

options.text: Send all logs to a dedicated logging account that application account administrators cannot access. Enable CloudTrail log file integrity validation. Store logs in S3 with Object Lock in Compliance mode (WORM). Use a separate IAM role in the logging account for log administration, with no cross-account access from application accounts. Enable S3 access logging on the log bucket itself.
Store logs in the same account as the application.
Use CloudWatch Logs with extended retention.
Export logs to an external SIEM solution only.

explanation: A dedicated logging account with restricted access prevents administrators from tampering with logs. S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode provides WORM storage that even the root user cannot override. CloudTrail integrity validation enables verification of log authenticity. S3 access logging provides an audit trail for log access. Option B allows administrators to modify logs. Option C can be modified by account admins. Option D depends on external availability.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to implement a strategy for managing multiple versions of an API simultaneously. The existing API must continue serving clients while a new version is being developed and tested. Which approach BEST supports this with API Gateway?

options.text: Use API Gateway stages to manage API versions. Deploy the existing API to a 'v1' stage and the new version to a 'v2' stage. Use stage variables to configure different Lambda function versions or backend endpoints for each stage. Implement custom domain names with base path mappings to route /v1 and /v2 to the respective stages.
Create separate API Gateway APIs for each version.
Use query string parameters to differentiate API versions.
Deploy only the latest version and require all clients to update.

explanation: API Gateway stages with custom domain base path mappings provide clean API versioning. Stage variables allow different backend configurations per version. Both versions are served simultaneously from the same API Gateway with different base paths. Option B duplicates API definitions. Option C is non-standard for versioning. Option D breaks existing clients.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to implement a solution for managing application configuration across multiple environments that supports configuration hierarchy and inheritance. Environment-specific values should override default values. Which approach provides this capability?

options.text: Use AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store with parameter hierarchies. Organize parameters as /app/default/key and /app/production/key. The application first reads environment-specific parameters and falls back to defaults. Use SecureString parameters for sensitive values. Implement parameter versioning for change tracking and rollback.
Use separate configuration files for each environment stored in S3.
Hard-code configuration values with environment switches in the application code.
Use a single flat list of environment variables for all configurations.

explanation: Parameter Store hierarchies support organized, inheritable configuration. Applications read environment-specific parameters first and fall back to defaults. SecureString provides encryption for sensitive values. Versioning enables change tracking and rollback. IAM policies can restrict access by hierarchy path. Option B requires custom merging logic. Option C requires code changes. Option D lacks organization and inheritance.

stem: A company runs an event-driven architecture where events from multiple sources (API Gateway, S3, IoT) flow through Amazon EventBridge to trigger various processing workflows. They need to ensure no events are lost, even during downstream service failures. Which pattern provides the MOST reliable event processing?

options.text: Configure EventBridge rules with dead-letter queues (SQS) for failed event deliveries. Enable EventBridge Archive and Replay to store all events for replay if needed. Configure retry policies on EventBridge rules with exponential backoff. Use EventBridge Pipes with SQS as a buffer for critical event streams that require guaranteed delivery.
Increase the EventBridge service quota for PutEvents.
Log all events to CloudWatch Logs as a backup.
Use SNS instead of EventBridge for guaranteed delivery.

explanation: DLQs capture events that fail delivery after retries. Archive and Replay provides long-term event storage and replay capability. Retry policies with backoff handle transient failures. EventBridge Pipes with SQS buffer provide guaranteed delivery for critical streams. Option B does not address delivery failures. Option C logs events but cannot replay them. Option D does not provide archive/replay.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to create CloudWatch dashboards that automatically update when new resources are added or removed. Rather than manually updating dashboards, the dashboards should discover resources dynamically. Which feature supports this?

options.text: Use CloudWatch Explorer widgets in the dashboard that dynamically discover and display metrics from resources matching tag-based filters. As new resources are added with matching tags, they automatically appear on the dashboard. Combine with CloudWatch Metrics Insights queries that aggregate metrics across resources matching specific criteria.
Update dashboards manually when resources change.
Create a Lambda function that updates the dashboard definition periodically.
Use static metric widgets for all resources.

explanation: CloudWatch Explorer widgets use tag-based discovery to automatically include new resources matching the filter criteria. Metrics Insights queries provide dynamic aggregation across matching resources. Both eliminate manual dashboard maintenance. Option B is manual. Option C requires custom code. Option D requires updates for new resources.

stem: A DevOps team needs to implement canary-based health monitoring for their multi-Region application. If the primary Region's canary fails consistently, traffic should be automatically routed to the DR Region. What is the BEST implementation?

options.text: Create CloudWatch Synthetics canaries in each Region that test critical application workflows. Configure Route 53 health checks that monitor the canary's CloudWatch alarm. Use Route 53 failover routing policy with the health checks. When the primary Region's canary consistently fails, Route 53 automatically routes DNS to the DR Region.
Use ALB health checks only for failover decisions.
Monitor CloudWatch metrics and manually update DNS.
Use Global Accelerator health checks without synthetic monitoring.

explanation: Synthetics canaries provide deep application health monitoring by simulating user workflows. Route 53 health checks integrated with canary alarms enable automatic DNS failover. This provides end-to-end health validation before failover. Option B only checks endpoint availability, not application health. Option C is manual. Option D checks endpoint health without validating application functionality.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to implement a solution that automatically detects and blocks malicious IP addresses across all CloudFront distributions and ALBs in the organization. The solution must update block lists in near-real-time based on threat intelligence. What is the recommended approach?

options.text: Use AWS WAF with IP reputation lists (AWSManagedRulesAmazonIpReputationList). Additionally, create a Lambda function that processes GuardDuty findings and VPC Flow Log anomalies to identify malicious IPs, then updates a WAF IP set via the WAF API. Associate the WAF web ACL with all CloudFront distributions and ALBs using AWS Firewall Manager for centralized management across accounts.
Manually update WAF IP block lists when attacks are detected.
Use only AWS Shield for IP blocking.
Block IPs at the security group level across all instances.

explanation: AWS Managed Rules provide baseline IP reputation filtering. Lambda-driven dynamic IP set updates add custom threat intelligence from GuardDuty and Flow Logs. Firewall Manager ensures consistent WAF policy across all accounts and resources. Option B is slow and manual. Option C does not support custom IP blocking. Option D does not protect CloudFront and is difficult to manage at scale.

stem: A company needs to implement automated security scanning in their CI/CD pipeline. The scanning must include static application security testing (SAST), dynamic application security testing (DAST), and software composition analysis (SCA) for known vulnerabilities in dependencies. How should this be integrated?

options.text: Add CodeBuild stages for each scan type: SAST using CodeGuru Reviewer or a tool like SonarQube in CodeBuild, SCA using tools that check dependencies against vulnerability databases (e.g., Snyk, OWASP Dependency-Check in CodeBuild), and DAST using tools that scan the deployed staging environment. Gate production deployment on scan results using a manual approval or automated Lambda that checks scan findings.
Scan code only after it reaches production.
Use only Amazon Inspector for all security scanning.
Perform security scanning quarterly as part of compliance audits.

explanation: Integrating SAST, SCA, and DAST into the CI/CD pipeline provides comprehensive security scanning. SAST catches code-level vulnerabilities early. SCA identifies vulnerable dependencies. DAST tests the running application. Gating production deployment on results prevents vulnerable code from reaching production. Option B is too late. Option C only covers runtime vulnerability scanning. Option D is infrequent.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to implement a solution for managing Kubernetes Helm charts and deploying them to multiple EKS clusters across different environments. Charts must be versioned and deployments must be tracked. Which approach is MOST manageable?

options.text: Store Helm charts in an Amazon ECR OCI registry for versioned chart storage. Use a CodePipeline with CodeBuild stages that run 'helm upgrade --install' for each environment. Configure values files per environment (values-dev.yaml, values-staging.yaml, values-prod.yaml). Use Helm release history for rollback capability.
Apply raw Kubernetes YAML manifests using kubectl.
Store charts in S3 and deploy manually using helm commands.
Use CloudFormation to manage all Kubernetes resources.

explanation: ECR OCI registry provides versioned Helm chart storage integrated with AWS. CodePipeline with CodeBuild automates deployments across environments. Per-environment values files customize configurations. Helm release history enables rollback. Option B lacks templating and versioning. Option C is manual. Option D does not manage Kubernetes resources well.

stem: A company has a microservices architecture where Service A depends on Service B. When Service B is slow or unavailable, Service A's response times degrade significantly, causing cascading failures. How should the DevOps engineer implement resilience patterns in the application?

options.text: Implement retry with exponential backoff and jitter for transient failures. Add circuit breaker pattern that opens after a threshold of failures, returning a fallback response instead of waiting for Service B. Implement timeouts on all inter-service calls. Add bulkhead pattern to limit the number of concurrent calls to Service B, preventing resource exhaustion in Service A.
Increase the timeout for calls to Service B.
Add more instances of Service A to handle degraded performance.
Remove the dependency on Service B.

explanation: Retry with backoff and jitter handles transient failures without overwhelming Service B. Circuit breaker stops calling Service B when it is consistently failing, preventing cascading failures. Timeouts prevent indefinite waiting. Bulkhead limits concurrent calls to prevent resource exhaustion. Together these patterns provide comprehensive resilience. Option B makes cascading failures worse. Option C does not solve the dependency issue. Option D may not be feasible.

stem: A DevOps team manages an application with service level objectives (SLOs) that define acceptable error rates and latency targets. They need to implement SLO monitoring that calculates error budget consumption in real time. Which approach provides this?

options.text: Use CloudWatch metric math to calculate the error budget. Define the SLO as a target (e.g., 99.9% availability = 0.1% error budget). Use METRICS() and MATH expressions to calculate the current error rate over a rolling window. Create an alarm when the error budget burn rate exceeds a threshold. Visualize remaining error budget on a CloudWatch dashboard.
Monitor individual request metrics without aggregation.
Calculate SLO compliance manually at the end of each month.
Use AWS Trusted Advisor for SLO monitoring.

explanation: CloudWatch metric math enables real-time SLO calculation using expressions that compute error rates over rolling windows. Burn rate alarms detect rapid error budget consumption. Dashboard widgets visualize remaining budget. This implements SRE error budget practices natively in AWS. Option B lacks the aggregate SLO view. Option C is too infrequent. Option D does not monitor application SLOs.

stem: A company is experiencing intermittent Lambda function failures with 'Task timed out' errors. The function processes DynamoDB Stream events. The DevOps team needs to diagnose the root cause. What is the systematic diagnostic approach?

options.text: Enable X-Ray tracing on the Lambda function to visualize the call graph and identify which downstream calls are slow. Check CloudWatch Logs for the function to analyze execution patterns before timeouts. Review the DynamoDB Stream iterator age metric to detect if the function is falling behind. Check the function's concurrent execution metrics to see if throttling is contributing. Correlate timeout occurrences with DynamoDB throttling events.
Increase the Lambda timeout to the maximum of 15 minutes.
Rewrite the function in a different programming language.
Replace the Lambda trigger with a polling mechanism.

explanation: X-Ray identifies slow downstream calls causing timeouts. CloudWatch Logs reveal patterns in function execution. Iterator age shows if the function is processing events fast enough. Concurrent execution metrics identify throttling. DynamoDB throttling correlation identifies if read throttling is causing retries and timeouts. Option B masks the root cause. Option C does not address the diagnostic need. Option D changes the architecture unnecessarily.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to implement network isolation for sensitive workloads running on EKS. The sensitive pods must only communicate with specific namespaces and external endpoints. How should this be implemented?

options.text: Implement Kubernetes Network Policies using a CNI plugin that supports them (like Calico on EKS). Define ingress and egress network policies that restrict pod communication to specified namespaces and CIDR blocks. Use namespace labels for policy selectors. For external endpoint restriction, combine with AWS security groups for pods.
Use separate EKS clusters for sensitive workloads.
Use only Kubernetes RBAC to restrict network access.
Rely on VPC subnet isolation only.

explanation: Kubernetes Network Policies provide fine-grained network isolation at the pod level. Calico or similar CNI plugins enforce these policies on EKS. Namespace-based selectors group pods logically. Security groups for pods add VPC-level enforcement. Option B is expensive and operationally complex. Option C controls API access, not network traffic. Option D does not provide pod-level isolation.

stem: A DevOps team needs to implement a strategy for managing Lambda function deployments across multiple Regions for a global application. Each Region must run the same function version, and deployments must be coordinated. How should this be automated?

options.text: Use CodePipeline with cross-Region actions. The pipeline builds and packages the Lambda function once, then deploys to each Region sequentially using CloudFormation deploy actions with Region-specific configurations. Use CloudFormation StackSets as an alternative for simultaneous multi-Region deployment of Lambda resources.
Deploy Lambda functions manually in each Region.
Use Lambda@Edge for global deployment.
Create separate pipelines in each Region.

explanation: CodePipeline cross-Region actions enable a single pipeline to deploy to multiple Regions. Building once ensures consistency. CloudFormation StackSets can deploy Lambda resources across Regions and accounts simultaneously. Both approaches ensure coordinated, consistent deployments. Option B is manual. Option C is for CloudFront edge computing, not general Lambda. Option D requires managing multiple pipelines.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to implement a solution for automatically patching EC2 instances with zero downtime. The fleet runs behind an ALB and uses Auto Scaling. Patches must be applied during a defined maintenance window with automatic rollback if patching causes issues. What is the BEST approach?

options.text: Use AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager with maintenance windows. Configure patching to use a rolling approach: deregister instances from the ALB target group, apply patches, verify health, register back with ALB. Use SSM Automation to orchestrate the process. Configure Auto Scaling to temporarily increase capacity during patching to maintain availability.
Create new AMIs with patches and replace all instances at once.
SSH into instances and apply patches manually.
Disable Auto Scaling and patch instances one by one.

explanation: SSM Patch Manager with maintenance windows provides scheduled, automated patching. The rolling approach with ALB deregistration ensures zero downtime. Temporary capacity increase maintains availability during patching. SSM Automation orchestrates the multi-step process. Option B causes downtime during replacement. Option C is manual. Option D risks capacity issues.

stem: A company uses Amazon SQS to process asynchronous jobs. Some jobs fail permanently after multiple retries. The team needs to handle these failed jobs by notifying support, preserving the message for investigation, and providing a mechanism to reprocess them after the issue is fixed. Which architecture supports this?

options.text: Configure a dead-letter queue (DLQ) on the main SQS queue with a maxReceiveCount of 3. Create an EventBridge rule triggered by SQS messages arriving in the DLQ (using SQS event source). The rule triggers a Lambda function that: stores the message in DynamoDB for investigation, sends an SNS notification to support, and provides a reprocessing API that moves messages from DynamoDB back to the main queue.
Delete failed messages after maximum retries.
Increase the retry count to avoid messages going to the DLQ.
Log failed messages to CloudWatch Logs only.

explanation: DLQ captures permanently failed messages after retries. Lambda processing of DLQ messages enables notification and persistence. DynamoDB stores message details for investigation. A reprocessing API enables replay after fixes. Option B loses failed messages. Option C delays failure handling without solving the root cause. Option D only logs without supporting reprocessing.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to implement container logging for an EKS cluster with thousands of pods generating high-volume logs. The solution must be cost-effective while providing search capability for recent logs and long-term storage for compliance. What architecture should be used?

options.text: Deploy Fluent Bit as a DaemonSet on EKS for log collection. Configure Fluent Bit to send recent logs (last 30 days) to CloudWatch Logs for searching and alerting. Simultaneously send all logs to S3 via Kinesis Data Firehose for long-term, cost-effective storage. Use S3 lifecycle policies to transition older logs to S3 Glacier for compliance retention. Use Athena for ad-hoc queries on S3 logs.
Send all logs to CloudWatch Logs with maximum retention.
Use kubectl logs for accessing container logs.
Deploy an Elasticsearch cluster on EKS for log management.

explanation: Fluent Bit is lightweight and efficient for high-volume log collection. Dual output to CloudWatch (recent, searchable) and S3/Firehose (long-term, cheap) optimizes cost. S3 lifecycle policies manage long-term retention. Athena enables ad-hoc queries on archived logs. Option B is expensive for high volume. Option C is limited and ephemeral. Option D requires managing infrastructure.

stem: A company needs to implement automated response to AWS Trusted Advisor checks that identify underutilized resources (idle EC2 instances, unattached EBS volumes, idle load balancers). The response should notify resource owners and optionally stop or terminate idle resources after a grace period. What is the BEST implementation?

options.text: Use Trusted Advisor's integration with EventBridge to capture check results. Create EventBridge rules that trigger a Step Functions workflow: identify the resource owner from tags, send notification via SNS with a deadline for response, tag the resource as 'pending-cleanup', wait for the grace period using a Step Functions Wait state, check if the tag has been removed (indicating owner action), and stop/terminate the resource if no action was taken.
Review Trusted Advisor recommendations weekly and act manually.
Immediately terminate all flagged resources.
Disable Trusted Advisor checks to avoid generating recommendations.

explanation: EventBridge integration enables automated response to Trusted Advisor findings. Step Functions orchestrates the multi-step workflow with notification, grace period, and conditional cleanup. Tag-based owner identification and communication provide a fair process. The Wait state handles the grace period natively. Option B is manual and delayed. Option C may terminate needed resources. Option D removes visibility.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to implement secure access to Amazon RDS databases for developers and applications without managing database passwords. The solution should use temporary credentials and integrate with IAM. Which approach is correct?

options.text: Enable IAM database authentication on the RDS instance. Create IAM policies that grant rds-db:connect permission with the database user specified in the resource ARN. Generate IAM authentication tokens using the AWS SDK and use them as passwords when connecting to the database. Tokens are valid for 15 minutes and renewed automatically by the SDK.
Store database passwords in Secrets Manager and share them with developers.
Use the RDS master user credentials for all access.
Create individual database users with passwords for each developer.

explanation: IAM database authentication eliminates password management. IAM policies control database access using standard IAM mechanisms. Authentication tokens are temporary (15 minutes) and generated via the AWS SDK. Connection is encrypted via SSL. Option B still manages passwords. Option C shares a privileged account. Option D requires managing database user credentials.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to implement a strategy for testing infrastructure changes in isolation before applying them to shared environments. Each developer should be able to spin up a complete test environment that mirrors production. What is the MOST cost-effective approach?

options.text: Create a parameterized CloudFormation template or CDK app that provisions a complete environment. Use CodeBuild triggered by feature branch pushes to deploy ephemeral environments using the branch name as a stack name suffix. Configure a scheduled Lambda function to automatically tear down environments for branches that have been inactive for over 24 hours.
Maintain permanent test environments for each developer.
Share a single test environment among all developers.
Test changes directly in the staging environment.

explanation: Ephemeral environments provide isolated testing without permanent infrastructure costs. Branch-based naming enables multiple concurrent environments. Automatic teardown prevents cost overruns from forgotten environments. CloudFormation ensures environments mirror production. Option B is expensive. Option C causes conflicts. Option D risks the shared staging environment.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to implement a blue/green deployment strategy for an RDS database schema migration. The migration adds new columns and modifies existing queries. How should this be performed with zero downtime?

options.text: Use Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments to create a green environment (clone of the production database). Apply schema migrations to the green database. Test the new application version against the green database. When validated, use the RDS switchover operation to promote the green environment to production with minimal downtime (typically under 1 minute).
Run ALTER TABLE statements directly on the production database during off-hours.
Create a manual database snapshot, restore it, and switch the application.
Use DMS to migrate data to a new database with the updated schema.

explanation: RDS Blue/Green Deployments create a staging environment synchronized with production via logical replication. Schema changes are applied to the green environment safely. The switchover operation promotes green to production with minimal downtime. This is the AWS-native zero-downtime migration approach. Option B risks production data integrity. Option C requires manual coordination. Option D is complex for schema migration.

stem: A company runs a real-time analytics application that processes events from Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. The application must continue processing during Region-level failures. How should cross-Region resilience be implemented for the streaming pipeline?

options.text: Configure producers to write to Kinesis streams in both the primary and DR Regions simultaneously (dual-write pattern). In the DR Region, keep consumer applications deployed but paused. Use Route 53 health checks to monitor the primary Region's processing health. When failover is triggered, activate the DR Region consumers. Implement deduplication logic in consumers to handle the overlap during failover.
Use Kinesis Data Streams cross-Region replication.
Store all events in S3 and process them after a Region failure.
Rely on a single Region and accept data loss during failures.

explanation: Dual-write to both Regions ensures no data loss during failover. Pre-deployed but paused consumers in the DR Region enable fast activation. Route 53 health checks trigger automated failover. Deduplication handles the overlap period. Option B does not exist as a native Kinesis feature. Option C introduces processing delays. Option D accepts data loss.

stem: A DevOps team needs to implement application performance monitoring (APM) that provides code-level insights including function execution times, database query performance, and external API call durations. Which AWS-native solution provides this?

options.text: Use AWS X-Ray with the X-Ray SDK integrated into the application code. Instrument incoming requests, downstream HTTP calls, database queries, and AWS SDK calls. Use X-Ray service maps to visualize dependencies. Analyze X-Ray traces to identify slow segments. Create X-Ray groups for filtering traces by URL, status code, or latency. Configure sampling rules to balance detail with cost.
Use CloudWatch metrics for application performance.
Add timing logs to every function manually.
Use VPC Flow Logs to analyze network performance.

explanation: X-Ray provides code-level APM with segment and subsegment timing for requests, downstream calls, and database queries. Service maps visualize application topology. Trace analysis identifies performance bottlenecks at the code level. Groups and sampling rules manage data volume and cost. Option B provides infrastructure metrics only. Option C is manual and inconsistent. Option D only shows network traffic.

stem: A company detects unusual outbound data transfer from their VPC to an unknown external IP address. This could indicate data exfiltration. What immediate actions should the DevOps engineer take?

options.text: Analyze VPC Flow Logs to identify which EC2 instances are communicating with the external IP. Check GuardDuty findings for related threat detections. Update NACL or security groups to block the external IP. Isolate suspected compromised instances using forensic security groups. Capture EBS snapshots and memory dumps for evidence. Review CloudTrail for unauthorized API calls from the suspected instances' roles.
Block all outbound traffic from the VPC immediately.
Wait for GuardDuty to generate a finding before acting.
Terminate all running instances in the VPC.

explanation: VPC Flow Logs identify the source instances. GuardDuty provides threat context. Blocking the specific IP contains the threat without disrupting legitimate traffic. Instance isolation preserves evidence while stopping exfiltration. EBS snapshots and memory dumps provide forensic data. CloudTrail reveals potential compromise scope. Option B disrupts all services. Option C delays response. Option D destroys evidence.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to implement a solution for securely distributing and rotating TLS certificates for services running in Amazon ECS. The certificates are used for mutual TLS (mTLS) between microservices. Which approach provides the MOST automated certificate lifecycle management?

options.text: Use AWS Private Certificate Authority (PCA) to issue private certificates for mTLS. Integrate PCA with AWS App Mesh, which automatically requests and rotates certificates using Envoy proxies. Configure App Mesh virtual nodes with TLS settings that reference the PCA. Envoy handles certificate rotation transparently without application changes.
Generate self-signed certificates and distribute them via S3.
Use ACM public certificates for inter-service communication.
Manually create and distribute certificates to each container.

explanation: AWS PCA with App Mesh provides fully automated private certificate lifecycle management. App Mesh's Envoy proxies handle certificate issuance, distribution, and rotation automatically. No application code changes needed. PCA issues short-lived certificates that are rotated before expiration. Option B lacks automation and lifecycle management. Option C is for public-facing services. Option D is manual and error-prone.

stem: A DevOps team needs to implement a deployment strategy for a stateful application running on EC2 instances with local data. The deployment must not lose any local data and must maintain application availability. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Use CodeDeploy with an in-place deployment type. Configure the appspec.yml with lifecycle hooks: ApplicationStop to gracefully stop the application, BeforeInstall to back up local data, AfterInstall to restore data and configure the new version, ValidateService to verify the application is functioning correctly. Use a deployment configuration with minimum healthy instances.
Use Blue/Green deployments that create new instances.
Replace instances with a new launch template version.
Use immutable deployments that replace the entire fleet.

explanation: In-place deployment with CodeDeploy preserves local data because the same instances are updated. Lifecycle hooks manage the data backup/restore process. ApplicationStop ensures graceful shutdown. BeforeInstall backs up data. AfterInstall restores data with the new version. ValidateService verifies functionality. Option B creates new instances that lose local data. Option C replaces instances. Option D replaces the fleet.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to implement a solution for managing and enforcing AWS account baseline configurations. Every new account in the organization should automatically receive: a CloudTrail trail, VPC with standard CIDR, Config recorder, GuardDuty enablement, and IAM password policy. What is the MOST automated approach?

options.text: Use AWS Control Tower Account Factory for Terraform (AFT) or Control Tower Account Factory to provision new accounts with standardized baselines. Define the baseline using CloudFormation StackSets with service-managed permissions and auto-deployment to organization units. When a new account is created and added to an OU, StackSets automatically deploy all baseline resources.
Write a runbook for manually configuring each new account.
Create an AMI with all configurations for the account.
Use a Lambda function that runs monthly to check account configurations.

explanation: Control Tower (or AFT) with StackSets provides fully automated account baselining. When accounts are created and added to OUs, StackSets automatically deploy baseline CloudFormation stacks. Control Tower provides additional guardrails and governance. This ensures every account is configured from creation. Option B is manual and error-prone. Option C does not apply to account configuration. Option D has a delay and is reactive.

stem: A company needs to implement a multi-Region active-active architecture for an application using DynamoDB and ECS. Both Regions must serve read and write traffic. Which TWO configurations are essential for data consistency?

options.text: Enable DynamoDB Global Tables to replicate data between Regions with eventual consistency. Implement conflict resolution in the application using the last-writer-wins strategy based on the aws:rep:updatetime attribute.
Use Route 53 latency-based routing to direct users to the nearest Region. Configure health checks for both Regions to enable automatic failover if one Region becomes unhealthy.
Use DynamoDB Streams with Lambda to replicate data manually.
Use a single-Region DynamoDB table with cross-Region VPC peering.
Implement synchronous replication between Regions for strong consistency.

explanation: DynamoDB Global Tables provide multi-Region replication for active-active write capability. Last-writer-wins conflict resolution handles concurrent writes. Route 53 latency-based routing sends users to the nearest Region for best performance, with health check-based failover for resilience. Option C duplicates Global Tables functionality.
